lesson.title: Turning Hunches Into Evidence: The Scientific Method in Psychology
lesson.summary: This section explains how psychologists convert an everyday hunch about behavior into a testable, falsifiable claim, and why that process is what separates psychological science from opinion.
lesson.body:
Imagine two people arguing about whether playing violent video games makes someone more aggressive. One insists it obviously does, since the games simulate violence. The other insists it obviously does not, since millions of people play them without ever hurting anyone. Both feel completely certain, and both cannot be right simply because they feel certain. This is the exact kind of disagreement that pushed psychology to adopt the scientific method, a systematic process for turning a hunch about behavior into a claim that can be tested, supported, or ruled out with evidence rather than settled by gut feeling or personal experience alone.

The scientific method follows a predictable sequence. It starts with an observation that raises a question, moves to a hypothesis, a specific and testable prediction about what should happen if the idea is correct, and then requires an operational definition, a precise statement of exactly how each concept will be measured. Aggression is too vague to study directly, so a researcher might operationally define it as the number of times a participant chooses to blast a stranger with a loud, unpleasant noise during a lab task. Once the hypothesis and definitions are set, researchers collect data, analyze it statistically, and draw a conclusion about whether the evidence supports or contradicts the original prediction.

Psychologists have several tools for gathering that evidence, and each comes with real tradeoffs. Descriptive methods, including case studies, naturalistic observation, and surveys, are useful for describing behavior in rich detail but cannot explain why it happens. Correlational research measures whether two variables rise and fall together, which is great for spotting patterns, but a correlation never proves that one thing causes another. Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together across the year, not because ice cream causes drowning, but because a third variable, summer heat, drives both. Only the experimental method, in which researchers manipulate an independent variable, measure its effect on a dependent variable, and randomly assign participants to conditions to rule out competing explanations, can establish cause and effect.

A hypothesis only counts as scientific if it is falsifiable, meaning some possible result would have to be able to prove it wrong. A claim that fits every outcome no matter what happens is not testable, so it is not science, no matter how reasonable it sounds. This is also why psychologists never treat a single striking result as the final word. Findings must be replicated, meaning independent researchers repeat the study and check whether they get similar results, before the field accepts a claim as reliable knowledge rather than a fluke.

This method is what turns psychology from a collection of opinions into a science, and it is the toolkit that makes everything else in this course possible. Every debate we cover, including the long running question of how much of who we are comes from genes versus environment, gets settled not by which explanation sounds more convincing, but by which one survives careful, falsifiable, and repeatable testing.
